title: Earth as a System: Energy, Matter, and Life

sections.title: Interaction of Solar Radiation on the Earth's Surface
Uneven Heating Causes Wind and Ocean Currents

slides.title: Sunlight: Energy for Earth
bullets: Solar radiation is the main source of energy on the Earth.
It reaches us as electromagnetic (EM) waves that travel through a vacuum at the speed of light.
Unlike EM waves, sound waves from Chapter 10 are mechanical waves and need a medium to travel.
The speed of light in vacuum is 3 x 10^8 m/s.
slides.note: Sooraj ki energy vacuum mein bhi travel karti hai, no medium needed!

slides.title: The Electromagnetic Spectrum
slides.kicker: From gamma rays to radio waves
bullets: EM waves cover a wide range of frequencies, from high frequency gamma rays and X-rays to low frequency infrared and radio waves.
High frequency EM waves like gamma rays and X-rays have very high energy and can be harmful for life on Earth.
About 99 per cent of the Sun's energy reaching Earth falls in the ultraviolet, visible and infrared range.
Microwaves and radio waves carry very little energy that can significantly warm the Earth.

left.title: High frequency
items: very high energy, can harm life

slides.title: How Each Ray Behaves
bullets: Short wavelength UV is mostly absorbed by the ozone layer in the upper atmosphere, protecting life and adding some atmospheric heating.
Visible light reaches the surface and powers photosynthesis, the primary source of food for most organisms, and partly warms land and water.
Infrared radiation warms the surface, which then re-radiates this heat back into the atmosphere.
Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour trap a portion of the outgoing heat, keeping Earth warm enough for life.

slides.title: Insolation and UV Facts
slides.kicker: Insolation warms land, air and you
bullets: The amount of the Sun's radiation that reaches the Earth's surface is called insolation.
Insolation is responsible for warming the Earth's surface and its atmosphere.
UV rays lie in the wavelength range of 100 nm to 400 nm and have much higher energy than visible light.
Long UV exposure can damage eyes and skin and raise cancer risk, yet UV also kills germs in water purifiers and powers fluorescent lights.

left.title: UV risks
items: raises cancer risk on long exposure

slides.title: Surfaces Heat Up Differently
slides.kicker: Colour and material decide the heat
bullets: Different materials absorb and heat up differently under sunlight.
You have already learnt that land heats up faster than water, with variation due to the land material and the colour of the soil.
Dark surfaces absorb more sunlight, so dark coloured roads heat up more quickly.
Light coloured surfaces reflect more sunlight and stay cooler, which is why dark clothes feel hotter than white ones in summer.

left.title: Dark surfaces
items: dark roads and dark clothes feel hotter

slides.title: Albedo: The Whiteness Factor
bullets: The fraction of solar radiation reflected by a surface is called its albedo.
High albedo surfaces stay cool because they reflect more light.
Low albedo surfaces reflect less and absorb more, so they heat up more quickly.
Snow and ice have high albedo, keeping polar regions very cold, while black soil and ocean water have lower albedo and stay warmer.
slides.note: Activity 13.2: find the albedo of everyday objects!

slides.title: Night Heat Re-radiation
slides.kicker: Why some houses stay cool at night
bullets: All objects radiate heat, which you have learnt in earlier grades.
We feel hot inside a concrete house at night during hot summer because of the heat re-radiated by the concrete.
Traditional houses built with thick mud and wooden walls offer cool conditions even in hot summer due to less re-radiation.

slides.title: Urban Heat Island Effect
bullets: Cities are warmer than their surrounding rural areas, especially during summer and at night.
Buildings of steel, concrete and brick, and roads made of concrete and asphalt, absorb solar radiation and retain heat.
The re-radiated heat from these materials warms cities more than the surrounding rural areas.
This raises energy demand for air conditioning, further stressing urban ecosystems.

slides.title: A Spherical Earth Angles Rays
bullets: The Earth is spherical, so the Sun's rays strike different latitudes at different angles.
Radiation falling on the equatorial region is concentrated over a smaller area.
In the polar region the same radiation is spread over a larger area.
This is why equatorial regions remain relatively warm throughout the year while polar regions stay much colder.

left.title: Equator
items: energy concentrated on a smaller area

right.title: Poles
items: energy spread over a larger area

slides.title: Warm Equator, Cold Poles
bullets: Uneven heating creates temperature differences between the equator and the poles.
These temperature differences between latitudes are the starting point for large scale movement of air and water.
Solar radiation is not evenly distributed across the globe.

slides.title: Tilt, Seasons, Global Circulation
bullets: The Earth's spherical shape and the tilt of its axis of rotation give rise to seasons.
They also change the length of daytime during one revolution of the Earth around the Sun.
Because solar radiation is spread unevenly, this uneven heating drives global winds and ocean currents.

slides.title: Meet the Atmosphere
slides.kicker: Gravity holds an ocean of air
bullets: The air surrounding the Earth is called the atmosphere, and it is held in place by the force of Earth's gravity.
It consists mainly of nitrogen (78 percent) and oxygen (21 percent).
Small amounts of argon, carbon dioxide, water vapour and other gases are also present.

slides.title: Troposphere: Weather's Home Layer
bullets: The atmosphere has a layered structure that helps explain key weather patterns.
Nearly all weather phenomena take place in the troposphere, which has an average height of about 12 km.
This layer is heated from the Earth's surface, and temperature decreases with height at about 6.5 degrees Celsius per km.
As warm air rises it drives winds and storms; the troposphere is tallest above the equator and lowest above the polar regions.

slides.title: Stratosphere and Layers Above
bullets: In the stratosphere (12 to 50 km) the ozone layer absorbs UV rays and heats the atmosphere, so temperature rises with height.
This increase in temperature with height calms the layer due to lack of vertical mixing, keeping weather confined to the troposphere.
Above it, the mesosphere, thermosphere and exosphere play only a minor role in regulating climate at the surface.
At about 100 km above the Earth begins the region we call outer space.

items: Troposphere 0 to 12 km: weather forms, temperature falls with height
Stratosphere 12 to 50 km: ozone absorbs UV, temperature rises with height
Mesosphere, thermosphere, exosphere: minor climate role
About 100 km up: outer space begins

slides.title: Meet a Scientist: Ramanathan
bullets: K. R. Ramanathan, India's atmospheric scientist, climbed to 18000 feet in the Himalayas in 1934 to measure ozone levels.
He discovered the levels were lower than expected.
His work laid the foundation for understanding how UV absorption varies with altitude and pollution.
Later, he led early monsoon forecasting efforts.
slides.note: Scientist banke pahad chadhna, that is dedication!

slides.title: The Atmosphere's Two Shield Jobs
bullets: Firstly, it partly absorbs incoming solar radiation: the ozone layer blocks harmful UV rays, and clouds and gases absorb some sunlight.
Secondly, it traps outgoing heat radiated from the warmed surface.
These two roles show how the atmosphere regulates energy flow, shaping weather, climate and life.

left.title: Blocks incoming
items: clouds and gases absorb some sunlight

right.title: Traps outgoing
items: keeps Earth warm enough for life

slides.title: Wind: High to Low
bullets: Wind is the movement of air from a region of high pressure to a region of low pressure.
These pressure differences are mainly caused by the uneven heating of the Earth's surface by the Sun.

items: Air moves from high to low pressure

slides.title: Land, Water and Breezes
bullets: Uneven heating of land and water is also responsible for phenomena such as land and sea breezes, which you have studied earlier.
The pressure differences behind these breezes come from the same source: the Sun heating different surfaces unequally.

slides.title: Same Idea, Bigger Scale
slides.kicker: From a sea breeze to oceans
bullets: The same basic idea of uneven heating and pressure difference helps us understand winds and ocean currents on vastly different scales.
A breeze in your town and a current crossing an ocean are cousins driven by the same mechanism.

slides.title: Valley Breeze: Daytime Climb
slides.kicker: Morning air walks up the slopes
bullets: In mountainous regions, the slopes and the valley floor do not heat up and cool down at the same rate.
During the day, mountain slopes facing the Sun are heated more rapidly than the valley floor.
Air over the slopes becomes warm and rises, creating a low pressure region.
Cooler air from the valley moves up the slopes to replace the rising warm air; this flow is called a valley breeze.

items: Slopes facing the Sun heat faster
Warm air over slopes rises, low pressure forms
Cooler valley air flows up the slopes
This daytime flow is the valley breeze

slides.title: Mountain Breeze: Night Flow
slides.kicker: Night air slides into the valley
bullets: After sunset, the situation reverses in the mountains.
The mountain slopes lose heat faster and become cooler, while the valley floor remains relatively warmer.
Air over the slopes becomes cooler and denser and flows down into the valley.
This downhill night flow is known as a mountain breeze.

items: After sunset slopes lose heat faster
Air over slopes cools and becomes denser
Dense air flows down into the valley
This night flow is the mountain breeze

slides.title: Breezes in Himalayan Valleys
bullets: Such daily changes in wind direction are commonly experienced in hilly regions like Shimla, Dehradun and other Himalayan valleys.
The wind reverses twice a day: up the slopes by day, down into the valley at night.

right.title: Mountain breeze: night
items: air moves down into the valley

slides.title: Small Winds, Big Roles
slides.kicker: Local winds quietly run mountain life
bullets: Local winds influence the weather conditions, agriculture and daily life in mountainous regions.
They help regulate temperature and moisture conditions and support soil and crop health.
Uneven heating of the Earth's surface sets up these winds, an important part of the Earth's atmospheric circulation.

flashcards.front: What is the main source of energy on the Earth?
flashcards.back: Solar radiation. It reaches the Earth as electromagnetic waves travelling through a vacuum at the speed of light.

flashcards.front: Define insolation.
flashcards.back: The amount of the Sun's radiation that reaches the Earth's surface; it warms the surface and the atmosphere.

flashcards.front: Which three spectrum regions carry about 99 percent of the Sun's energy to Earth?
flashcards.back: Ultraviolet, visible and infrared. Microwaves and radio waves carry very little warming energy.

flashcards.front: Name the greenhouse gases listed in the chapter.
flashcards.back: Carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour. They trap a portion of the outgoing heat and keep Earth warm enough for life.

flashcards.front: What is albedo and where does the word come from?
flashcards.back: The fraction of solar radiation reflected by a surface. The word comes from Latin and means whiteness.

flashcards.front: Why do polar regions remain very cold?
flashcards.back: Snow and ice have high albedo, so they reflect a large proportion of the incoming solar radiation.

flashcards.front: Why does a concrete house feel hot at night in summer?
flashcards.back: Concrete re-radiates the heat it absorbed during the day, warming the house at night.

flashcards.front: What is the urban heat island effect?
flashcards.back: Cities stay warmer than rural areas, especially in summer and at night, because steel, concrete, brick and asphalt absorb and retain heat.

flashcards.front: Why is the equator warmer than the poles?
flashcards.back: Sun's radiation is concentrated over a smaller area at the equator but spread over a larger area in the polar region.

flashcards.front: Which two features of the Earth give rise to seasons?
flashcards.back: Its spherical shape and the tilt of its axis of rotation, acting during one revolution around the Sun.

flashcards.front: What does uneven heating across the globe drive?
flashcards.back: It drives global winds and ocean currents across the Earth.

flashcards.front: What holds the atmosphere around the Earth?
flashcards.back: The force of Earth's gravity holds the air surrounding the Earth, which we call the atmosphere.

flashcards.front: Which two gases make up almost all of the atmosphere?
flashcards.back: Nitrogen (78 percent) and oxygen (21 percent), with small amounts of argon, carbon dioxide and water vapour.

flashcards.front: In which layer does nearly all weather take place?
flashcards.back: The troposphere, with an average height of about 12 km, heated from the Earth's surface.

flashcards.front: Why does temperature rise with height in the stratosphere?
flashcards.back: The ozone layer there absorbs UV rays and heats up the atmosphere, so temperature increases with height.

flashcards.front: Define wind.
flashcards.back: Wind is the movement of air from a region of high pressure to a region of low pressure.

flashcards.front: What mainly causes pressure differences on the Earth?
flashcards.back: The uneven heating of the Earth's surface by the Sun.

flashcards.front: Which familiar phenomenon shows uneven heating of land and water?
flashcards.back: Land and sea breezes, which you have studied earlier.

flashcards.front: What is a valley breeze?
flashcards.back: A daytime flow in which cooler air from the valley moves up the slopes to replace rising warm air.

flashcards.front: What is a mountain breeze?
flashcards.back: A night flow in which cooler, denser air over the slopes flows down into the valley.

flashcards.front: Name two hilly places where these daily wind changes are felt.
flashcards.back: Shimla and Dehradun, along with other Himalayan valleys.

quiz.q: Solar radiation reaches the Earth in the form of which waves?
options: Electromagnetic waves travelling through a vacuum
quiz.why: EM waves travel through vacuum at the speed of light, unlike mechanical sound waves from Chapter 10.

quiz.q: What is the speed of light in vacuum?
quiz.why: The book states the speed of light in vacuum is 3 x 10^8 m/s.

quiz.q: Which type of solar radiation is mostly absorbed by the ozone layer?
quiz.why: Short wavelength UV is mostly absorbed by the ozone layer in the upper atmosphere, protecting life.

quiz.q: About what percentage of the Sun's energy reaching Earth falls within UV, visible and infrared wavelengths?
quiz.why: About 99 per cent of the Sun's energy falls in the UV, visible and infrared range.

quiz.q: How does infrared radiation help keep the Earth warm enough for life?
options: It is reflected back by clouds into space
The surface re-radiates it and greenhouse gases trap a portion of the outgoing heat
It converts carbon dioxide into oxygen
It speeds up evaporation from oceans
quiz.why: Infrared warms the surface; CO2, methane and water vapour trap a portion of this outgoing heat.

quiz.q: A surface with high albedo will most likely:
options: Absorb more light and heat up quickly
Reflect more light and stay cooler
quiz.why: Albedo is the reflected fraction; high albedo surfaces reflect more and stay cool.

quiz.q: Which of these surfaces has low albedo and stays relatively warmer?
quiz.why: Black soil and ocean water absorb more solar radiation, so they are relatively warmer.

quiz.q: On a hot summer night, why do traditional mud and wooden houses feel cooler than concrete houses?
options: Wood produces a cooling breeze inside
Concrete re-radiates stored heat while thick mud and wood re-radiate less
Concrete conducts the cold from the sky
quiz.why: The book attributes the coolness of mud and wood houses to less re-radiation at night.

quiz.q: Compared with the poles, sunlight falling on the equatorial region is:
quiz.why: At the equator the radiation is concentrated over a smaller area, keeping it warm all year.

quiz.q: Polar regions experience much colder conditions mainly because:
options: Their night lasts a whole month
Sun's radiation is spread over a larger area there
Ocean currents carry all their heat away
The atmosphere is missing above the poles
quiz.why: Rays strike different latitudes at different angles, spreading polar radiation over a larger area.

quiz.q: Which combination correctly explains the seasons and changing day length?
options: Change in the Sun's energy output over a year
Distance change from the Sun during revolution
Spherical shape plus tilt of the axis during one revolution around the Sun
Only the tilt of the axis, with no revolution
quiz.why: The book credits the Earth's spherical shape and tilted axis of rotation during one revolution.

quiz.q: The atmosphere stays around the Earth because of:
quiz.why: The air surrounding the Earth is held in place by the force of Earth's gravity.

quiz.q: Roughly what fraction of the atmosphere is nitrogen?
quiz.why: Nitrogen makes up 78 percent and oxygen 21 percent, with small amounts of other gases.

quiz.q: How does temperature change with height in the troposphere?
options: It increases by about 6.5 degrees C per km
It stays the same at all heights
It decreases at about 6.5 degrees C per km
quiz.why: The troposphere is heated from the surface, so temperature decreases with height, about 6.5 C per km.

quiz.q: Why is there little vertical mixing of air in the stratosphere?
options: Ozone makes the air heavier at the bottom
Temperature rises with height as ozone absorbs UV, calming the layer
Strong planetary winds flatten the layer
The stratosphere contains almost no gases
quiz.why: Rising temperature with height calms the stratosphere, keeping weather confined to the troposphere.

quiz.q: Wind always moves air from:
quiz.why: Wind is the movement of air from a region of high pressure to a region of low pressure.

quiz.q: The pressure differences that create winds are mainly caused by:
options: Uneven heating of the Earth's surface by the Sun
quiz.why: The book states pressure differences are mainly caused by uneven heating of the surface by the Sun.

quiz.q: Which statement correctly links small and large scale circulation?
options: The same uneven heating idea explains land and sea breezes as well as winds and ocean currents on vastly different scales
Breezes need mountains while winds need deserts
Ocean currents are caused only by the Moon
Local and global winds follow completely unrelated causes
quiz.why: The same basic idea of uneven heating works on vastly different scales, from breezes to ocean currents.

quiz.q: During the day in a mountain valley, the cooler air typically flows:
options: Up the slopes from the valley
quiz.why: Warm air rises over heated slopes, so cooler valley air moves up as the valley breeze.

quiz.q: A mountain breeze forms at night because:
options: The valley floor cools faster than the slopes
Slopes lose heat faster and their cool dense air flows down into the valley
The Moon heats the mountain slopes
quiz.why: After sunset slopes cool first; the denser air over them flows down into the warmer valley.

quiz.q: Why do local winds matter to people in hilly regions?
options: They cause the seasons to change
They regulate temperature and moisture and support soil and crop health
quiz.why: Local winds influence weather, agriculture and daily life, regulating temperature, moisture, soil and crop health.

examples.title: Which roof stays cooler under the same Sun?
examples.problem: Two terrace roofs in the same colony receive the same sunlight. One roof is painted light in colour and the other is dark like a black road. Using the idea of albedo, predict which roof stays cooler and explain why.
steps: Albedo is the fraction of solar radiation reflected by a surface; the word comes from Latin and means whiteness.
A light coloured surface has high albedo, so it reflects more sunlight and absorbs less, just like snow and ice that reflect a large proportion of incoming radiation and keep polar regions cold.
A dark surface has low albedo, like black soil and ocean water, so it reflects less, absorbs more solar radiation and heats up more quickly.
This matches what you see daily: dark coloured roads heat up quickly and dark clothes feel hotter than white ones in summer.
examples.answer: The light coloured roof stays comparatively cooler because its high albedo reflects more sunlight; the dark roof absorbs more radiation and heats up faster.

examples.title: How much cooler at the top of the troposphere?
examples.problem: The troposphere has an average height of about 12 km, and its temperature decreases with height at about 6.5 degrees Celsius per km. Estimate how much cooler the air at the top of the troposphere is compared with the air at the surface.
steps: Rate of temperature decrease with height = 6.5 degrees Celsius per km.
Average height of the troposphere = 12 km.
This falling temperature with height is why warm air rises, driving winds and storms in this layer; the layer is tallest above the equator and lowest above the polar regions.
examples.answer: The top of the troposphere is about 78 degrees Celsius cooler than the surface (6.5 x 12 = 78).

examples.title: One day of breezes in a Himalayan valley
examples.problem: A student spends a full day in Shimla. Describe the direction of the wind in the valley from afternoon to late night, naming each breeze and explaining the heating pattern that causes it.
steps: In the afternoon, mountain slopes facing the Sun are heated more rapidly than the valley floor.
The air over the slopes becomes warm and rises, creating a low pressure region, so cooler air from the valley moves up the slopes. This daytime flow is the valley breeze.
After sunset the situation reverses: the slopes lose heat faster and become cooler, while the valley floor remains relatively warmer.
The air over the slopes becomes cooler and denser and flows down into the valley. This night flow is the mountain breeze.
examples.answer: Afternoon: valley breeze blows up the slopes from the valley. Late night: mountain breeze blows down into the valley. The direction reverses daily, as commonly experienced in Shimla, Dehradun and other Himalayan valleys.

steps.label: Sun sends energy
steps.detail: Solar radiation travels as electromagnetic waves through vacuum at the speed of light.

steps.label: Atmosphere filters rays
steps.detail: Ozone absorbs most UV; clouds and gases absorb some incoming sunlight.

steps.label: Surface absorbs unevenly
steps.detail: Albedo, land versus water and colour decide how much heat each place keeps.

steps.label: Latitude spreads heat
steps.detail: Equator gets concentrated rays; poles get rays spread over a larger area.

steps.label: Pressure differences form
steps.detail: Warm air rises leaving low pressure; cooler air flows in from high pressure.

steps.label: Winds begin to blow
steps.detail: Local breezes near mountains and larger winds circle the globe.

steps.label: Ocean currents flow
steps.detail: Strong planetary winds drag surface water, moving huge ocean masses.

steps.label: Matter cycles link spheres
steps.detail: Water, carbon and nitrogen circulate between air, life, soil and rocks.

steps.label: Life stays in balance
steps.detail: Greenhouse gases keep Earth warm enough while cycles renew matter for life.
